explanations.explanation: God says it twice in one verse: “for they are a rebellious house.” Their eyes and ears work fine, so the trouble isn't their equipment. I think that's what makes it sting. You can have perfect hearing and still not want to listen, and I know a few snooze buttons that prove it.

Distance isn't it, friend. God tells Ezekiel, “you are living in a rebellious house,” so these people are right there with him. That's about as close as you can get to a neighbor. The reason God gives is “for they are a rebellious house.”

That's a kind guess, but God never says anything about a lack of news. The reason He gives is plain: “for they are a rebellious house.” Notice that the verse is about eyes and ears that work and still don't take it in. So the problem He names isn't missing information.

That's the trip. God says, “pack your bags for exile,” and later, “go out like those who go into exile” (Ezekiel 12:3-4). Exile means being forced away from home, so this is no vacation. Ezekiel is a man with a suitcase and a very serious message.

A feast would be a happy reason to pack, and I'd bring the cookies. But God doesn't say feast here. He says, “pack your bags for exile.” Exile is leaving home as people carried away, so there's no party at the end of this road.

War packing looks different, friend. God says this is a bag for exile: “Bring out your baggage for exile by day, as they watch.” Nothing in these verses sends Ezekiel to fight anybody. He's acting out a man being led away from home.

God doesn't promise that, baker. He says, “Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious house.” That word “Perhaps” matters a lot here. It leaves the door open without saying they'll walk through it.

Right, because God is careful with His words here. He says, “Perhaps they will understand, though they are a rebellious house.” “Perhaps” isn't “for sure,” and the verse keeps that difference. Ezekiel still packs the bags in full view, and that's his job.

explanations.answer: So he cannot see the land
explanations.explanation: Yes, God says, “cover your face so that you cannot see the land.” Ezekiel carries his bags out at dusk, and the covered face is part of the picture. Walking out with a blindfold-like cover on your face is a hard way to leave a place. Later God says the prince will do the very same thing (Ezekiel 12:12).

That's a sneaky-sounding guess, but the text gives a different reason. God says, “cover your face so that you cannot see the land.” The point is what Ezekiel can't see, not who can see him. Besides, everybody is watching him do this on purpose.

My mustache would vote for dust protection, I'll admit it. But God gives the reason Himself: “cover your face so that you cannot see the land.” It's about not seeing, not about keeping clean. Ezekiel is already digging through a wall by hand, so I think dust is the least of his worries.

Yes, God says, “For I have made you a sign to the house of Israel.” A sign points at something beyond itself. Ezekiel's packing, wall digging and face covering are all pointing at what's coming for Jerusalem. He's the signpost, and he doesn't get to say a word until God sends the explanation.

Ezekiel isn't being put in charge of anybody here. He's carrying a suitcase through a hole in a wall, which is not a throne room. God says, “I have made you a sign to the house of Israel.” The only ruler in these verses is the prince, and that comes later.

I see why you'd say it, since he does look like a stranger leaving town. But God's word is “sign”: “For I have made you a sign to the house of Israel.” A stranger is just somebody new. A sign is something that points to a message, and that's the job Ezekiel was given.

Yes, and the text says it right away: “So I did as I was commanded.” Ezekiel brings the bags out by day, digs through the wall in the evening and carries his things out at dusk. Nobody likes digging through their own wall, and he did it anyway. That's obedience with drywall dust on it.

The text says the opposite, friend. Ezekiel reports, “So I did as I was commanded.” He brought out his bags by day and dug through the wall in the evening. The orders were strange, and he followed every one.

explanations.answer: The prince in Jerusalem and the people there
explanations.explanation: That's it. God says, “This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are there.” A burden here is a heavy message from the LORD. Ezekiel is acting it out in front of the exiles, but the message is about the people back in Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: The exiles living right there with Ezekiel
explanations.explanation: That makes sense, since they're the ones watching. But God points somewhere else: “This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are there.” The word “there” means Jerusalem, not the crowd standing around Ezekiel. The audience is here, and the message is about people far away.

explanations.answer: The kings of the nations around Israel
explanations.explanation: No foreign kings are in this one. God says, “This burden concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel who are there.” The prince is the one from Jerusalem, and the people are the house of Israel. The neighbors' thrones aren't part of this message.

Yes, God says, “they will go into exile as captives.” Ezekiel's act is a preview. “Just as it happened here, so will it be done to them.” Captives don't choose the trip, which makes it very different from packing for a vacation.

Pilgrims travel to somewhere holy because they want to go. God's word is “captives”: “they will go into exile as captives.” That one word tells you they won't be heading out freely. It's a heavy one, so I'll just say it plainly.

Settlers pick a spot and unpack, like somebody who's excited about a new kitchen. But God says, “they will go into exile as captives.” They aren't choosing where to land. Captives get carried, and settlers get to decide.

Yes, God says, “I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My snare.” The prince slips out of the city with his face covered, but he doesn't get away. A net is something you can't just walk out of. That's the picture God paints.
A cloak sounds cozy, and I like cozy. But God says what He'll spread over the prince: “I will spread My net over him.” A cloak covers you, and a net catches you. This verse is about the catching.

Wings do sound lovely, like something warm to hide under. But in this verse God says, “I will spread My net over him, and he will be caught in My snare.” It's a net, and it's meant to hold him. It's not the shelter you were picturing.

God says something very different. He'll bring the prince to Babylon, “yet he will not see it, and there he will die.” That fits the covered face from verse 12, where the prince covers it “so he cannot see the land.” It's a heavy verse, and I think it's a hard one to sit with.

Right. God says, “I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, and there he will die.” The Chaldeans are the people who live in Babylon. It's a heavy verse, so I'll leave it quiet.

explanations.answer: So they can recount their abominations among the nations
explanations.explanation: Yes, God says He'll spare a few “so that in the nations to which they go, they can recount all their abominations.” Then He adds, “Then they will know that I am the LORD.” So the few who are left will tell the story in the places they're scattered to. It's a small group carrying a big message.

explanations.answer: So they can rebuild the ruined altars of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Rebuilding sounds hopeful, but that's not what this verse says. God spares a few “so that in the nations to which they go, they can recount all their abominations.” The survivors are headed for the nations, and the verse has them telling, not building. Altars never come up.

explanations.answer: So they can bring offerings to the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's a good-sounding job, but it isn't the one God names. He spares a few so that “in the nations to which they go, they can recount all their abominations.” These survivors are scattered among the nations. The verse gives them one task, and it's telling.

That's it. God tells Ezekiel, “eat your bread with trembling, and drink your water with quivering and anxiety.” This time there's no wall and no suitcase. It's just a man at a meal, shaking, in front of everybody. Even a plain lunch becomes part of the message.

I'd love to eat a cookie with gladness, believe me. But God says, “eat your bread with trembling.” The whole picture is about worry, not cheer. Later the people in Jerusalem are told they'll “eat their bread with anxiety” (Ezekiel 12:19).

Patience is a nice way to eat, but God asks for something shakier. He says, “eat your bread with trembling, and drink your water with quivering and anxiety.” Trembling is the opposite of calm. Ezekiel is acting out how scared the people in Jerusalem will be.

Yes, God says the land “will be stripped of everything in it because of the violence of all who dwell in it.” He names the reason Himself, and it's about how the people lived. I think it's a heavy verse, and I won't joke about the reason. The land is stripped because of what the people did.

Poverty isn't the word God uses. He says the land “will be stripped of everything in it because of the violence of all who dwell in it.” The cause He names is violence. That tells us the stripping comes from how the people lived, not from being short on money.

Sickness is a natural guess for a land in trouble. But God says it plainly: the land “will be stripped of everything in it because of the violence of all who dwell in it.” Violence is the cause. Sickness doesn't show up in that verse.

God says the opposite. In verse 20 He says, “The inhabited cities will be laid waste, and the land will become desolate.” So the cities don't get to stand there untouched while the land suffers. It's all part of the same picture.
Right. God says, “The inhabited cities will be laid waste, and the land will become desolate.” Cities and land go down together. Then He adds, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.”

Yes. The proverb says, “The days go by, and every vision fails,” which means time keeps passing and nothing happens. God answers it in the next verses, saying “every vision will be fulfilled” (Ezekiel 12:23). So He takes the claim head on.

Not quite, friend. The proverb says, “The days go by, and every vision fails,” and “the days go by” sounds like a lot of waiting. God's answer is that “every vision will be fulfilled” (Ezekiel 12:23). Nobody in that saying is complaining about speed.

explanations.answer: The visions are hard to understand
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to say about some visions, but the proverb isn't about that. It says, “The days go by, and every vision fails.” That's about visions not coming true. God's reply isn't a better explanation either, because He says “every vision will be fulfilled” (Ezekiel 12:23).
Yes. God says, “I will put an end to this proverb, and in Israel they will no longer recite it.” He doesn't just argue with it. He ends it. Then He gives them a new line to say instead.

The text says the opposite, baker. God says, “I will put an end to this proverb, and in Israel they will no longer recite it.” The saying about failing visions is the one that goes away. God doesn't let it stand.

That's what He says: “For there will be no more false visions or flattering divinations within the house of Israel.” A flattering divination is a message that tells people what they want to hear. God says that kind is over. He puts it right next to His promise that His own word will be fulfilled.

The text says the other way. God says, “For there will be no more false visions or flattering divinations within the house of Israel.” Flattering divinations are messages that only tell people what they want to hear. God says those are done.

Yes, God says, “because I, the LORD, will speak whatever word I speak, and it will be fulfilled without delay.” Think of the proverb about the days going by. Here God says His word won't be held up. A cookie timer I trust, and this word I trust a whole lot more.

Witnesses would make a nice crowd, but God doesn't mention them here. He says His word “will be fulfilled without delay.” The point of the verse is about timing, not who's watching. That fits what the people were saying about waiting.

It's a smart-sounding guess, since God does warn them through Ezekiel. But the verse says His word “will be fulfilled without delay.” The word is “delay.” It answers the people who think the visions are taking forever.

Close, but they don't say never. They say, “The vision that he sees is for many years from now; he prophesies about the distant future.” That's “far off,” not “won't happen.” God's answer is, “None of My words will be delayed any longer.”

Right. The saying is, “The vision that he sees is for many years from now; he prophesies about the distant future.” They're pushing it far away, which is different from saying it will never happen. God answers, “None of My words will be delayed any longer.”
